newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan refugee returns to village and new fears.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugee returns to village and new fears.

text.p: Paul Ndaibakunze, his wife and five children returned from two-and-a-half years of exile in Zaire to find their home destroyed and world upside down.
Thick weeds stood tall in the house's four rooms and overgrowth covered crumbling mud walls.
"The bush has taken it back," said Ndaibakunze, sweating from a seven km (five-mile) climb from the border to his hillside village. "No roof, no windows, no doors. There is nothing left."
Ndaibakunze, 36, and his wife Saida Nyirandageya, 35, their faces deeply lined, looked much older than their years standing outside the ruin, surrounded by giant, untended banana groves.
Soon after they left in July 1994, Rwanda's rich, red earth on the steep hill choked drainage channels with dirt and weeds. leaving no escape for rainwater, which streamed into the house.
In the empty months that followed, looters came and took away everything, down to window frames, doors and the iron roof.
"I had no idea. We hadn't heard a word from Rubona because everyone fled with us," said Ndaibakunze. The same happened to four nearby homes whose owners also trickled back on Tuesday.

Ndaibakunze, balding and wearing a ragged suit jacket and dirt-encrusted shirt, climbed to the top of the hill and met the sons of a neighbour who died before 1994. They gave him use for 15 days of their late father's abandoned house four doors down.
"If we don't find somewhere by then we will have to sleep outside. We have no money," said Ndaibakunze, formerly a mechanic at the power company. He has been told his old job is filled.

Ndaibakunze had other setbacks in the new Rwanda, where the Tutsi minority seized power in 1994 for the first time since independence in 1964 after the killings of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis by Hutus who then fled into exile.
Forced out of a refugee camp on Friday, Ndaibakunze found it hard to reconcile his old and new lives dominated by forces way beyond his control.

"We left Mugunga (refugee camp) because the Zairean army surrounded us and soldiers we didn't know came and freed us. They call themselves the Banyamulenge (Zairean Tutsis) and we were overjoyed," he said as his family began patching up their temporary home.

Asked if the Hutu soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen behind the 1994 genocide had also returned since Friday with the flood of refugees, Ndaibakunze saw no reason to follow the standard response of most Hutus that they had escaped deeper into Zaire.
"They all came back to Rwanda together with us. Only a few stayed in Zaire. The others are here now in Rwanda," he said.
Most Tutsis in the border town of Gisenyi are sure former Hutu soldiers and Interahamwe are hiding among the refugees but say they are slowly being uncovered by genocide survivors.

Asked what he would do if a Tutsi stole his small plot of land, Ndaibakunze said: "When we came back to Rwanda we decided to stick to the law. If a Tutsi comes, I wouldn't fight for my land because he would be coming to fight for the government."
The government, which came to power with the Tutsi rebel victory in 1994, says land and houses should be returned to the returnee owners and warns against mob justice for suspects.

Ndaibakunze and his family registered with authorities in Nyamyumba commune on Tuesday and at a public meeting were assured by officials they were welcome and no action would be taken against returnees who took no part in the genocide.
The returnees and Tutsis who had moved into the area since 1994 even had a meal together as a step towards reconciliation.
Asked if he would, as required by law, tell the authorities if he saw any member of the Interahamwe returning to his village, Ndaibakunze said: "If he really killed he has to be punished."
But pressed on whether he would denounce him, he said: "No. If he escaped he could return and then kill me and my family."
